content.title: About
content.content: Brussels sprouts (Brassica oleracea var. gemmifera) are small, leafy green buds that grow along the sides of a tall stalk. They look like miniature cabbages and belong to the cruciferous family. They have a nutty, slightly bitter flavor that becomes sweeter when roasted, and they are eaten cooked or shaved raw.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Brussels sprouts are named after Brussels, Belgium, where they were widely cultivated.
They belong to the same species as cabbage, broccoli, kale, and cauliflower.
A single plant can produce dozens of sprouts along one stalk.
Roasting caramelizes their natural sugars and reduces bitterness.
Brussels sprouts are a cool-season crop, and light frost can make them taste sweeter.

items.title: Rich in vitamin K and vitamin C
items.content: Brussels sprouts are an excellent source of vitamin K for normal blood clotting and vitamin C for immune support.

items.title: Provides folate and potassium
items.content: These nutrients support cell function and normal blood pressure.

items.title: Provides dietary fiber
items.content: Brussels sprouts contribute fiber that supports normal digestion.

items.title: Contains glucosinolates
items.content: These plant compounds, found in cruciferous vegetables, are being studied for their protective activity.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Brussels sprouts are low in calories and filling.

items.title: Gas and bloating
items.content: Brussels sprouts can cause gas or bloating in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Thyroid considerations
items.content: Cruciferous vegetables contain compounds that may affect thyroid function in very large amounts. People with thyroid conditions should consult a healthcare professional.

items.title: Possible medication interactions
items.content: Brussels sprouts contain vitamin K. People taking blood thinners should consult a healthcare professional about keeping their intake consistent.

items.title: Overcooking
items.content: Overcooked sprouts can become bitter, mushy, and strong-smelling.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Brussels sprouts can be halved and roasted until crisp at the edges, steamed, sautéed, boiled, or shaved raw into salads. Trim the stem end and remove any loose outer leaves before cooking. Pairing them with olive oil, garlic, lemon, or nuts balances their bitterness.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unwashed Brussels sprouts in the refrigerator in a perforated bag, where they usually keep for about a week. Wash them just before use. They can also be blanched and frozen.

content.title: About
content.content: Cashew butter is a spread made by grinding cashew nuts into a smooth paste. It has a delicate creamy flavor with a hint of natural sweetness and a nutty aroma. Cashew butter is popular in vegan cooking, used in sauces, desserts, and as a butter substitute.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cashews originate from tropical regions of Africa but are now cultivated mainly in Southeast Asia and South America.
Cashews belong to the Anacardiaceae family and are more closely related to mangoes than to typical nuts.
Raw cashews contain urushiol, a toxic compound, so they are sold only after roasting or other processing.
Cashew butter is a staple in Asian cuisines, especially in Thai curries and sauces.
Unlike many peanut butters, cashew butter is often sold without added sugar or salt.

items.title: Rich in monounsaturated fats
items.content: Monounsaturated fats support heart health and help maintain healthy cholesterol levels.

items.title: Source of magnesium and copper
items.content: Magnesium aids muscle and nerve function, while copper is essential for red blood cell formation.

items.title: Contains vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is important for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Antioxidant content
items.content: Cashew butter provides tocopherols and phenolic compounds that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Energy support
items.content: Its high calorie density and healthy fats make it a good source of sustained energy for active individuals.

items.title: Tree nut allergy
items.content: Cashews can trigger severe allergic reactions in people with nut allergies.

items.title: High in calories
items.content: Because of its energy density, portion sizes should be moderated to avoid excess calorie intake.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Cashews contain oxalates, which may contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible individuals.

items.title: Raw nut toxicity
items.content: Unprocessed cashews contain urushiol and should only be consumed after proper heating.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cashew butter can be spread on toast, added to smoothies, sauces, oatmeal, baked goods, and desserts. It is also used as a vegan butter alternative. Gently warming the butter improves its pourability.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cashew butter in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For longer shelf life, keep it refrigerated – this helps preserve flavor and prevents oxidation. Discard if it develops a rancid smell or changes color.

classic-mixed-vegetables-canned-cooked-w.title: Classic mixed vegetables, canned, cooked with butter or margarine

content.title: About
content.content: Classic mixed vegetables are a canned blend of carrots, peas, corn and beans cooked in butter or margarine. The product is ready to eat, retains a bright colour, tender texture and a characteristic buttery flavour.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Vegetables are canned immediately after processing, preserving most of their vitamins and minerals.
Butter or margarine is added to enhance taste and increase the energy value of the product.
Canned mixes are popular for camping, work lunches and school meals because of their long shelf life.
The blend typically contains carrots, peas, corn and beans in a ratio that provides a balanced flavour.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: The vegetables provide vitamin B6 and folate, which support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Source of dietary fibre
items.content: Fibre aids normal digestion and helps maintain a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Beta‑carotene from carrots and lutein from corn protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Energy dense
items.content: Added butter or margarine raises the calorie content, making the product a good energy source for active individuals.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The mix supplies potassium, magnesium and iron, essential for electrolyte balance and blood formation.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Butter or margarine increases saturated fat levels, so people monitoring cholesterol should consume the product in moderation.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: Canned foods often contain added salt; individuals with hypertension should check the sodium content.

items.title: Margarine allergy
items.content: Margarine may contain soy or dairy ingredients that can trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: After opening
items.content: Once opened, the can should be transferred to a sealed container and kept in the refrigerator, used within 3‑4 days.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The product is ready to eat straight from the can. It can be added to salads, pasta, rice, omelets or served as a side dish with meat. If desired, gently warm the vegetables in a pan.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the unopened can in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep it refrigerated in an airtight container and consume within 4 days.

lamb-or-mutton-rice-and-vegetables-inclu.title: Lamb or Mutton with Rice and Vegetables

content.title: About
content.content: Lamb (or mutton) is the meat of sheep, known for its rich flavor and aroma. Combined with boiled rice and vegetables such as carrots, broccoli, and dark‑green leafy greens, the dish provides a balanced source of protein, carbohydrates, vitamins, and minerals.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Lamb contains more iron than beef, making it helpful for preventing anemia.
In Mediterranean cuisine, lamb is traditionally seasoned with rosemary, thyme, and mint.
Rice is one of the oldest cultivated crops, grown for over 5,000 years.
Broccoli is high in glucosinolates, compounds that support the body’s detoxification processes.
Dark‑green leafy vegetables like spinach and kale provide over 10 million IU of vitamin A per 100 g.

items.title: Rich source of high‑quality protein
items.content: Lamb supplies complete animal protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: High in iron and zinc
items.content: These minerals support immune function and normal nervous system activity.

items.title: Complex carbohydrates
items.content: Rice delivers steady energy, while fiber from the vegetables helps regulate blood sugar.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Lamb and rice provide vitamin B12, niacin, and riboflavin, important for metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Broccoli and leafy greens are rich in vitamin C, carotenoids, and polyphenols that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: High saturated fat content
items.content: Some cuts of lamb are rich in saturated fats; choose lean cuts and consume in moderation.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: A minority of people may experience allergic reactions to sheep meat.

items.title: Purine content
items.content: Lamb contains purines, which can raise uric acid levels in individuals prone to gout.

items.title: Contamination risk
items.content: Improper storage or undercooking can allow bacterial growth such as Salmonella.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Lamb can be roasted, braised, or pan‑seared and served with boiled rice and lightly sautéed vegetables. Add spices like cumin, coriander, and garlic to enhance flavor. Cook vegetables "al dente" to retain crunch and nutrients.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep raw lamb refrigerated at ≤ 4 °C for no more than 2‑3 days, and store cooked dishes in airtight containers for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze the meat in airtight bags and the prepared meal in portioned containers for up to 2 months.

macaroni-or-noodles-with-cheese-whole-gr.title: Macaroni or noodles with cheese, whole grain

content.title: About
content.content: Whole‑grain macaroni or noodles with a cheese sauce is a nutritious dish that combines whole‑grain pasta with a creamy dairy flavor. The whole‑grain pasta retains bran and germ, providing more fiber and micronutrients than refined white pasta.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Whole‑grain pasta contains two to three times more fiber than regular white pasta.
Cheese sauce is often made from real cheese, milk, and a small amount of flour, giving a rich, creamy texture.
In some countries whole‑grain pasta is marketed as “whole‑grain pasta” and used in traditional recipes.
The combination of complex carbs and protein makes this dish a good energy source for athletes.
When stored properly, dry pasta can keep its quality for up to two years.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain pasta provides both soluble and insoluble fiber, supporting digestive health and helping to regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Complex carbs deliver sustained energy, which is beneficial for endurance and steady performance.

items.title: Contains protein
items.content: The cheese sauce adds dairy protein, contributing to muscle repair and maintenance.

items.title: Calcium and vitamin D
items.content: Cheese sauce is a good source of calcium and, when fortified, vitamin D, supporting bone health.

items.title: Beneficial micronutrients
items.content: Whole‑grain pasta supplies iron, magnesium, and B‑vitamins that are important for metabolism.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Cheese sauce can trigger allergic reactions in individuals with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Prepared cheese sauces often contain a lot of salt; people monitoring sodium intake should choose low‑salt versions.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The dish can be calorie‑rich due to cheese and butter, so portion control is advisable for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Traditional pasta contains gluten; those with celiac disease need a gluten‑free alternative.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the macaroni hot, tossed with the cheese sauce. Add vegetables such as broccoli, spinach, or mushrooms, and optionally grilled chicken or turkey for extra protein. Top with grated Parmesan or fresh herbs for flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry pasta in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. Cooked pasta with sauce should be kept in the refrigerator for no more than 3‑4 days in a sealed container. Reheat to at least 75 °C before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Shrimp Egg Foo Yung is a classic Chinese-American dish consisting of a fluffy egg omelet filled with shrimp, vegetables, and served with a savory soy‑based sauce. It first appeared on menus in the United States around 1969 and quickly became a staple in Chinese take‑out restaurants.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish originated in California in 1969 and helped popularize the “American‑Chinese” cuisine trend.
Traditional recipes include shrimp, eggs, scallions, carrots, and sometimes bean sprouts.
The omelet is usually pan‑fried in a generous amount of oil, giving it a crisp golden crust.
In the U.S. it is commonly served with a thick dark soy sauce sweetened with a touch of sugar.
The name “foo yung” comes from Cantonese “fu yung,” meaning “egg prepared as an omelet.”

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Shrimp and eggs provide high‑quality protein essential for muscle repair and growth.

items.title: Contains omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Shrimp are a good source of EPA and DHA, which support heart and brain health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs and shrimp supply B12, B6, and riboflavin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The dish provides iron, zinc, and selenium, nutrients that aid immune function and antioxidant defense.

items.title: Low in carbs
items.content: When prepared with minimal sauce, it fits well into low‑carbohydrate eating plans.

items.title: Shellfish allergy
items.content: Shrimp can trigger severe allergic reactions in susceptible individuals.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: The accompanying sauce is often salty; people with hypertension should limit portion size.

items.title: Fried in oil
items.content: Traditional pan‑frying adds calories and may introduce trans fats.

items.title: Foodborne illness
items.content: Undercooked eggs can harbor salmonella; ensure the omelet is fully set.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve hot, sliced into strips, typically alongside steamed rice or noodles. Garnish with chopped scallions, cilantro, and a drizzle of chili sauce if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Refrigerate leftovers in an airtight container for 2‑3 days. Freeze for up to one month, though the texture of the omelet may become softer after thawing.

stewed-dried-beef-puerto-rican-style.title: Stewed Dried Beef, Puerto Rican Style

content.title: About
content.content: Stewed dried beef, Puerto Rican style, is a traditional snack from Puerto Rico. Beef strips are first dried to remove moisture and then slowly stewed in a sauce made from soy sauce, vinegar, garlic, oregano, and spices, giving it a rich, slightly sweet, and aromatic flavor. It is usually served cold in thin slices.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: It is a staple of “apetitos,” the small bites served with beer and cocktails in Puerto Rico.
The classic recipe uses a marinade of soy sauce, vinegar, garlic, oregano, and sometimes brown sugar.
Drying removes most of the water, while stewing re‑hydrates the meat and infuses it with flavor.
Often used in sandwiches, salads, and as a filling for empanadas.
Dried beef has a longer shelf life than fresh meat.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Provides complete animal protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Rich in iron
items.content: Contains heme iron, which is readily absorbed by the body.

items.title: Contains zinc
items.content: Zinc supports immune function and wound healing.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Supplies B12, niacin, and riboflavin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Suitable for low‑carb diets as it contains virtually no sugar.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: The salty marinade makes the product high in sodium, which may be a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Saturated fat
items.content: Beef contains saturated fat; people with heart disease should limit intake.

items.title: Beef allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to beef.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Commercial versions may contain additives such as nitrites that some consumers avoid.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy it as a snack, slice thinly for sandwiches, add to salads, use as a filling for empanadas, or serve with cheese and olives. It is typically served cold.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in an airtight container in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C for 2‑3 weeks. For longer storage, freeze in a moisture‑proof bag for up to 6 months. Discard if it develops an off‑odor or discoloration.
